content: 1. Survey Overview: The survey is a globally standardized tool aimed at understanding the drivers of childhood vaccination for children under the age of 5 (0–47 months). It includes 19 questions and is intended to be completed by parents or caregivers. The survey also includes a recommended consent script and socio-demographic questions, which can be adapted locally, but the core survey questions should remain unchanged. 2. Priority Indicators: The survey identifies five priority indicators for assessing vaccination uptake in children under 5. These indicators include: Confidence in vaccine benefits. Family norms regarding vaccination. Intention to vaccinate the child. Knowledge of where to access vaccination services. Affordability of vaccination. 3. Key Constructs and Questions: Confidence in Vaccine Benefits: Parents are asked how important they believe vaccines are for their child’s health. Responses are categorized as not at all important, a little important, moderately important, or very important. The percentage of parents who consider vaccines moderately or very important is recorded. Family Norms: Parents are asked if most of their close family and friends want them to vaccinate their child. Responses are recorded as yes or no. Intention to Vaccinate: Parents are asked if they want their child to receive all, some, or none of the recommended vaccines. The percentage of parents who want their child to receive all recommended vaccines is noted. Knowledge of Vaccination Sites: Parents are asked if they know where to take their child for vaccination. Responses are recorded as yes or no. Affordability: Parents are asked how easy it is to pay for vaccination, considering clinic fees, transportation costs, and time away from work. Responses range from not at all easy to very easy. 4. Additional Constructs: Confidence in Vaccine Safety: Parents are asked how safe they believe vaccines are for their child. The percentage of parents who consider vaccines moderately or very safe is recorded. Trust in Health Workers: Parents are asked how much they trust health workers who administer vaccines. Responses range from not at all to very much. Social Norms: Questions assess whether parents believe most other parents or community leaders support vaccination. Health Worker Recommendations: Parents are asked if a health worker has recommended vaccination for their child. Recall of Vaccination Reminders: Parents are asked if they have ever been contacted about their child being due for vaccination. 5. Practical Issues: Ease of Access: Parents are asked how easy it is to access vaccination services for their child. Responses range from not at all easy to very easy. Barriers to Access: Parents are asked to identify specific challenges, such as difficulty reaching the clinic, inconvenient clinic hours, being turned away, or long waiting times. Mother’s Travel Autonomy: Mothers are asked if they need permission to take their child to the clinic for vaccination. The percentage of mothers who do not require permission is recorded. Vaccination Availability: Parents are asked if they have ever been turned away from a clinic when trying to vaccinate their child. 6. Demographic Information: Age and Gender: The survey collects the age and gender of both the parent/caregiver and the youngest child. This allows for stratified analysis by age and gender. Relationship to Child: Parents are asked about their relationship to the child (e.g., mother, father, grandparent). Number of Children Under 5: Parents are asked how many children under 5 they have, with subsequent questions focusing on the youngest child. 7. Consent and Administration: Respondents can decline to answer any question or stop the interview at any time. Trained interviewers read the questions and response options aloud to respondents, emphasizing key words as needed. Instructions in square brackets or capital letters are not read aloud. 8. Rationale for Questions: Each question is designed to assess specific behavioral, social, or practical factors influencing vaccination uptake. For example: Questions about confidence in vaccine benefits and safety assess attitudes toward vaccination. Questions about family and social norms explore the influence of close contacts and community leaders. Questions about practical issues, such as affordability and ease of access, identify barriers to vaccination. 9. Data Collection and Analysis: The survey includes administrative questions for tracking purposes, such as participant ID, GPS coordinates, and date of the interview. Responses are analyzed to identify trends and barriers, enabling targeted interventions to improve vaccination coverage. 10. Adaptation and Use: While the survey is standardized, certain elements, such as the consent script and demographic questions, can be adapted to local contexts. This survey provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the factors influencing childhood vaccination uptake, enabling health programs to design targeted interventions to improve coverage.
